nodes.label: Bras, Kets, and Outer Products
nodes.explanation: Translate complex vectors and linear maps into bra-ket notation, distinguishing the scalar inner product from the operator outer product. Build and apply a rank-one projector in a two-dimensional example. Assume the calibrated ability to use complex-conjugate inner products, normalized vectors, and matrix eigenvectors; introduce the notation explicitly rather than reteaching those calculations. Leave changes of basis and the measurement postulate to their own lessons.

nodes.label: Adjoints and Hermitian Operators
nodes.explanation: Calculate an adjoint and determine whether a finite matrix is Hermitian, then explain why Hermitian eigenvalues are real and eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal. Use small complex matrices and distinguish Hermitian from merely real or symmetric. Assume the calibrated complex inner products and matrix eigenvalue skills. Establish the finite-dimensional result here; differential-operator boundary conditions and physical measurement rules come later.

nodes.label: Commutators and Operator Identities
nodes.explanation: Manipulate noncommuting products without changing their order, using commutator linearity and the product identities. Start with two explicit matrices, then practise deriving [N,a†]=a† from [a,a†]=I and N=a†a, without assuming oscillator physics. Assume ordinary matrix multiplication and algebra. The goal is reliable operator calculation; angular-momentum spectra and oscillator energy quantization are separate applications.

nodes.label: Global Phase, Relative Phase, and Interference
nodes.explanation: Distinguish a physically irrelevant overall phase from a relative phase that changes measurement probabilities. Use normalized two-component states and an explicitly supplied recombination matrix to predict interference, introducing Euler's formula as needed. Assume the calibrated Born-rule calculation and complex arithmetic, with no optics background. Do not infer an observable trajectory from interference or introduce time evolution yet.

nodes.label: Fourier Transforms and Wave Packets
nodes.explanation: Resolve a localized function into complex plane waves and reconstruct it using a consistent Fourier-transform convention. Work through a rectangular spectral amplitude and its spatial profile, introducing complex exponentials, inverse transforms, and norm preservation at a usable level. Assume the calibrated single-variable differentiation and integration; supply any additional integral identity. Interpret reciprocal widths without yet identifying wave number with momentum or proving quantum uncertainty.

nodes.label: Spherical Coordinates and Volume Elements
nodes.explanation: Convert Cartesian and spherical coordinates and integrate a three-dimensional density using d³r=r²sinθ dr dθ dφ. Derive the volume factor geometrically and distinguish radial density from density per unit volume using a simple rotationally symmetric example. Assume algebra, trigonometric functions, and single-variable integration; introduce iterated integrals explicitly. Differential operators and spherical harmonics are outside this lesson.

nodes.label: The Dirac Delta Distribution
nodes.explanation: Use the delta distribution under an integral to represent a point-supported source, including shifts and the scaling factor for a linear change of variable. Motivate it with unit-area narrow functions and distinguish its sampling rule from an ordinary function value. Assume the calibrated single-variable integration and introduce the limiting idealization explicitly without requiring formal convergence theory. Leave rigorous distribution theory, delta-potential eigenstates, and Green functions to later work.

nodes.label: Orthonormal Basis Expansions
nodes.explanation: Expand a state in an orthonormal basis, use completeness to reconstruct it, and calculate its coordinates in a different basis. Transform an operator matrix consistently and show why an inner product is independent of coordinates. Use two-dimensional examples to distinguish a physical state from its coefficient column. Generalized continuous bases and physical state evolution are not introduced here.

nodes.label: Spectral Projectors and Projective Measurement
nodes.explanation: Construct the spectral projectors of a Hermitian observable and use them to calculate outcome probabilities and the conditional state after an ideal projective measurement. Include a small degenerate eigenspace to show why an outcome need not select a unique eigenvector. Extend the already-known Born rule rather than repeating amplitude squaring. Specify the Lüders update for this ideal measurement model; general instruments come later.

nodes.label: Quantum Expectation Values and Variances
nodes.explanation: Compute an observable's ensemble mean and standard deviation from either its measurement distribution or its operator moments. Reconcile the two calculations in a small matrix example and distinguish an expectation value from a guaranteed individual outcome. Develop variance as the spread of outcomes in a prepared state. Begin with discrete spectra; continuous spatial probabilities receive their own treatment.

nodes.label: Compatible Observables and Common Eigenbases
nodes.explanation: Determine when two finite-dimensional Hermitian observables admit a common eigenbasis and construct one when degeneracy leaves a choice. Connect their vanishing commutator to compatible ideal measurements, distinguishing a shared eigenvector from a complete common basis. Practise with explicit matrices. Unbounded-operator domain subtleties and quantitative uncertainty bounds are outside this scope.

nodes.label: The Robertson Uncertainty Relation
nodes.explanation: Derive and apply ΔAΔB≥|⟨[A,B]⟩|/2 for a specified state, supplying the needed Cauchy–Schwarz argument from inner-product geometry. Use small Hermitian matrices to show that the lower bound can depend on the state and can vanish for noncommuting observables. Interpret preparation uncertainty rather than treating the bound as a universal statement about apparatus error. Position and momentum are applied later.

nodes.label: Unitary Operators and Reversible State Transformations
nodes.explanation: Test U†U=I and use a unitary matrix to transform states while preserving norms and transition probabilities. Distinguish an active physical transformation from a passive basis change, and find the inverse transformation. Work with small complex matrices rather than assuming matrix-exponential techniques. Identify what unitarity guarantees; Hamiltonian-generated evolution and measurement updates are separate concepts.

nodes.label: Time Evolution in an Energy Eigenbasis
nodes.explanation: Evolve an arbitrary superposition under a time-independent Hamiltonian by attaching e^(−iEₙt/ℏ) to each energy component. Introduce the Hamiltonian as the energy observable and solve the scalar Schrödinger equation for each coefficient, explaining ℏ and the complex-exponential solution. Practise a two-level transition probability in a different measurement basis. Distinguish stationary probabilities, overall phase, and evolving relative phase; spatial differential equations and driven Hamiltonians come later.

nodes.label: Position Measurements over Finite Intervals
nodes.explanation: Extend the projective Born rule to a wavefunction by calculating the probability of a finite position interval and the normalized state conditioned on that outcome. Distinguish density, probability, and their units, and calculate continuous position moments by integration. Assume the calibrated ability to normalize a sine wavefunction. Use finite detector regions so that an exact-position delta is not mistaken for a normalizable prepared state; momentum representations come next.

nodes.label: The Momentum-Space Wavefunction
nodes.explanation: Convert a position wavefunction into its momentum amplitude using p=ℏk and a stated Fourier convention, then calculate probabilities in momentum intervals. Introduce the de Broglie identification and explain why a plane wave has definite momentum but is not normalizable on the whole line. Use norm preservation to connect the two probability descriptions. Focus on changing representation; differential momentum operators and dynamics follow separately.

nodes.label: Canonical Position and Momentum Operators
nodes.explanation: Apply x̂ and p̂ in position and momentum representations and derive [x̂,p̂]=iℏ on an appropriate common set of smooth wavefunctions. Obtain p̂=−iℏ∂/∂x from plane-wave components and use operator integrals to calculate an observable moment. Explain the integration-by-parts identity and the role of boundary terms rather than assuming a course in functional analysis. Treat Hermiticity as domain-sensitive; rigorous self-adjoint extensions are excluded.

nodes.label: The Schrödinger Hamiltonian in Position Space
nodes.explanation: Construct H=−ℏ²∂²/(2m∂x²)+V(x) for a nonrelativistic particle and use it in the time-dependent Schrödinger equation. Explain mass, potential energy, p=mv, and the classical kinetic-energy expression needed to identify the quantum Hamiltonian; no prior mechanics course is assumed. Introduce partial derivatives through their concrete role and verify a supplied solution. Finding allowed eigenfunctions from boundary conditions is the next learning task.

nodes.label: Probability Current and the Continuity Equation
nodes.explanation: Derive the one-dimensional probability current from the Schrödinger equation and interpret the continuity equation as local conservation of probability. Calculate currents for right-moving, left-moving, and real stationary wavefunctions, distinguishing nonzero density from nonzero flux. Relate boundary flux to the probability inside an interval. Keep the treatment to real scalar potentials and defer reflection coefficients and three-dimensional cross sections.

nodes.label: Stationary Schrödinger Boundary-Value Problems
nodes.explanation: Turn a stationary-state problem into an eigenvalue boundary-value problem and choose oscillatory or exponential solutions according to E−V. Teach the constant-coefficient second-order differential-equation method explicitly using the calibrated differentiation skills. Apply normalizability and the matching conditions at finite potential steps, distinguishing them from hard-wall boundaries. The goal is to set up and check a physical eigenfunction; individual well spectra and scattering coefficients follow separately.

nodes.label: The Infinite Square Well
nodes.explanation: Derive the allowed energies and normalized eigenfunctions of a particle confined by two hard walls, then use the eigenfunctions to calculate spatial probabilities. Explain how boundary conditions select discrete energies and how a superposition differs from a single energy eigenstate. Reuse the learner's known sine-wave normalization rather than treating it as new mathematics. Finite penetration and scattering are excluded.

nodes.label: Bound States of the Finite Square Well
nodes.explanation: Match interior oscillations to exterior decaying tails and obtain the even and odd bound-state conditions of a symmetric finite square well. Explain even and odd functions directly and solve or bracket the resulting transcendental roots graphically. Interpret penetration depth and the finite number of bound levels. This lesson concerns discrete bound states, not incoming scattering waves or a general theory of parity operators.

nodes.label: Scattering from a Potential Step
nodes.explanation: Find reflected and transmitted amplitudes by matching stationary waves at a potential step and convert amplitudes into flux probabilities. Treat propagating and evanescent transmitted solutions to explain why T is not always the squared transmission amplitude and why an evanescent tail alone carries no transmitted current. Check R+T=1 for a real step. Finite-width barriers and multiple-interface resonances are deferred.

nodes.label: Tunneling through a Rectangular Barrier
nodes.explanation: Solve the two-interface matching problem for a finite rectangular barrier with incident energy below its height. Calculate transmission and explain how a nonzero transmitted flux can arise despite an exponentially suppressed interior wavefunction. Compare exact transmission with the thick-barrier exponential dependence and retain the distinction between amplitudes and fluxes. Above-barrier resonances and general smooth barriers are separate lessons.

nodes.label: Harmonic-Oscillator Ladder Operators and Energy Levels
nodes.explanation: Factor the harmonic-oscillator Hamiltonian using creation and annihilation operators and derive its discrete spectrum from the commutator and a lowest-energy state. Determine the normalized raising and lowering factors and use them to calculate simple x and p matrix elements in the number basis. Define the oscillator potential and frequency without assuming classical oscillation theory. Explicit coordinate wavefunctions and coherent states follow separately.

nodes.label: Harmonic-Oscillator Wavefunctions
nodes.explanation: Find the normalizable Gaussian ground state from the annihilation equation and construct the first excited coordinate wavefunctions with the raising operator. Recognize the Hermite-polynomial pattern, nodes, and parity without undertaking a separate special-functions course. Compare coordinate probabilities with number-state matrix calculations. Concentrate on the coordinate representation of already-derived energy states rather than deriving the spectrum again.

nodes.label: Free-Particle Wave-Packet Spreading
nodes.explanation: Evolve a localized free-particle packet by evolving its momentum components and transforming back to position space. Use a Gaussian example to calculate center motion and increasing width, supplying the Gaussian integral and explaining the algebra needed to use it. Distinguish phase velocity, group velocity, and dispersion through E=p²/(2m). Do not identify packet spreading with environmental decoherence or an increase in mixedness.

nodes.label: The Heisenberg Picture
nodes.explanation: Move time dependence from state vectors to operators using A_H=U†AU and verify that measurable expectations agree with the Schrödinger picture. Derive the operator equation of motion, including an observable's explicit time dependence, and solve a small matrix example. Keep the Hamiltonian time independent while explaining the representation change. Classical limits and splitting a Hamiltonian into free and driven parts are separate applications.

nodes.label: Ehrenfest's Theorem
nodes.explanation: Obtain equations for the mean position and momentum from the operator equation of motion for a particle in a potential. Explain the classical force relation F=−dV/dx and identify the additional approximation needed to replace ⟨V′(x)⟩ by V′(⟨x⟩). Use quadratic and nonquadratic examples to test when a mean trajectory obeys a closed classical equation. The theorem does not assert that every quantum state is a localized classical particle.

nodes.label: Unitary Symmetry Generators and Conservation Laws
nodes.explanation: Connect a continuous unitary transformation to its Hermitian generator and determine when that generator is conserved by checking its commutator with H. Derive spatial translations from the momentum operator and distinguish invariance of a Hamiltonian from invariance of a particular state. Introduce the infinitesimal expansion of an operator exponential directly. Rotation algebra and discrete parity receive separate treatments.

nodes.label: Parity Eigenstates and Parity Selection Rules
nodes.explanation: Apply the spatial-reflection operator, determine when it commutes with a Hamiltonian, and choose even or odd states in the resulting common eigenbasis. Use the transformation of an operator under parity to decide which matrix elements vanish without doing the integral. Explain how degeneracy limits the claim that every energy eigenvector has definite parity. Electric-dipole transitions and angular selection rules are developed later.

nodes.label: Minimum-Uncertainty Gaussian Wave Packets
nodes.explanation: Calculate Δx and Δp for a Gaussian and identify the uncorrelated Gaussian preparations that saturate ΔxΔp≥ℏ/2. Follow free evolution to distinguish minimum product uncertainty from a Gaussian with position-momentum correlations. Supply any needed Gaussian moment integral and interpret equality through the uncertainty derivation. Avoid presenting the preparation bound as a model of measurement disturbance.

nodes.label: Spin One-Half and Stern–Gerlach Measurements
nodes.explanation: Represent spin-one-half states and measurements with the Pauli matrices and predict probabilities for successive Stern–Gerlach filters along different axes. Introduce intrinsic angular momentum and explain the apparatus through its two spatial output channels without assuming electromagnetism coursework. Distinguish spin from literal rotation of a small object. Derive the needed matrix eigenstates explicitly; arbitrary angular-momentum representations and magnetic-field dynamics follow separately.

nodes.label: Spin Precession in a Constant Magnetic Field
nodes.explanation: Use H=−γ S·B to evolve a spin-one-half state in a uniform, constant magnetic field and calculate the time-dependent spin probabilities. Define the magnetic moment, gyromagnetic ratio, and field components needed by this model. Explain precession as changing relative phase rather than changing the probabilities in the energy basis. Oscillating fields and resonant driving are outside this lesson.

nodes.label: Angular Momentum as a Rotation Generator
nodes.explanation: Construct infinitesimal Cartesian rotations and use their noncommutativity to motivate [J_i,J_j]=iℏε_ijkJ_k. Define the index notation and required three-dimensional vector operations rather than assuming classical rigid-body mechanics. Show that J² commutes with each component while different components generally cannot have sharp values together. Establish the rotation algebra here; its allowed spectra are the next task.

nodes.label: Angular-Momentum Ladder Operators
nodes.explanation: Use J± and positivity of state norms to derive the joint J²,J_z eigenvalues and the allowed j,m ladders. Calculate normalized raising and lowering coefficients and construct a small-j operator representation. Distinguish integer and half-integer representations without assuming that every angular momentum is orbital. Coordinate eigenfunctions and addition of independent angular momenta require separate machinery.

nodes.label: The Three-Dimensional Schrödinger Equation
nodes.explanation: Build the scalar-potential Hamiltonian in three dimensions and apply the Cartesian or spherical Laplacian to a supplied wavefunction. Introduce gradients, partial derivatives in several variables, and the relevant Laplacian formulas explicitly, linking their use to the spherical volume element and normalization. Verify a simple separable solution without solving a new spectral problem. Angular eigenfunctions, central-potential separation, and electromagnetic vector potentials follow later.

nodes.label: Orbital Angular-Momentum Operators
nodes.explanation: Realize rotation generators as L=r×p acting on spatial wavefunctions and obtain usable expressions for L_z and L² in spherical coordinates. Define the cross product through its components and verify how these operators act on simple angular functions. Use single-valued spatial wavefunctions to explain the integer character of orbital angular momentum. Do not identify this restriction with the allowed intrinsic-spin representations; normalized spherical eigenfunctions come next.

nodes.label: Spherical Harmonics
nodes.explanation: Use Y_lm as the normalized joint eigenfunctions of orbital L² and L_z and interpret their angular probability distributions. Construct and normalize low-l examples, introducing the necessary Legendre-polynomial formulas and phase convention. Connect the coordinate functions to the abstract angular-momentum ladder coefficients. Focus on the angular basis and its orthogonality; radial dynamics and extensive special-function identities are excluded.

nodes.label: The Radial Schrödinger Equation for Central Potentials
nodes.explanation: Separate a rotationally invariant three-dimensional Hamiltonian into spherical harmonics and a radial equation. Use u(r)=rR(r) to obtain the effective one-dimensional equation with its centrifugal term, radial normalization, and origin boundary condition for regular potentials. Explain why the angular momentum changes radial motion even when the potential depends only on radius. Coulomb energy quantization and scattering asymptotics are subsequent applications.

nodes.label: Tensor Products of Quantum States and Operators
nodes.explanation: Build a joint Hilbert-space basis for two distinguishable systems, calculate product-state coefficients, and apply local operators such as A⊗I. Construct joint measurement projectors and distinguish a tensor product from an ordinary direct sum. Work with two finite systems so that the notation becomes computationally usable. Entanglement, particle indistinguishability, and reduced states are separate lessons rather than assumed meanings of the tensor product.

nodes.label: Center-of-Mass and Relative Coordinates
nodes.explanation: Transform a two-particle Hamiltonian with an interaction V(|r₁−r₂|) into center-of-mass and relative-motion terms and derive the reduced mass. Work through the coordinate derivatives and explain when the wavefunction can separate. Supply the elementary mass-weighted mechanical interpretation rather than assuming a prior two-body mechanics course. This method reduces an interacting pair to an effective one-body problem; it does not remove exchange symmetry requirements.

nodes.label: Frobenius Series for Bound-State Equations
nodes.explanation: Find an admissible leading power near a regular singular point, substitute a power series, and derive the coefficient recurrence for a second-order differential equation. Teach index shifting and coefficient comparison explicitly through a simple supplied radial-type equation. Relate local regularity to the eventual need for a globally normalizable solution. Develop this new solution method here so the Coulomb problem need not conceal an unfamiliar special-functions technique.

nodes.label: Hydrogenic Energy Quantization
nodes.explanation: Apply radial asymptotics and a terminating Frobenius series to the attractive Coulomb potential and derive the hydrogenic bound-state energies and allowed n,l values. Introduce the charge, Coulomb constant, Bohr length, and reduced-mass energy scale used in the calculation. Explain degeneracy in the scalar Coulomb Hamiltonian. Focus on nonrelativistic energy quantization; normalized orbital distributions, spin effects, and relativistic corrections come later.

nodes.label: Hydrogen Orbitals and Radial Probability
nodes.explanation: Build low-lying normalized hydrogenic orbitals from their radial factors and spherical harmonics, and calculate angular or radial probabilities. Introduce the needed associated-Laguerre polynomial formulas and work through 1s and representative n=2 examples. Distinguish |ψ|² from r²|R|² and a probability maximum from a definite electron position. Use already-established quantum numbers and energies rather than repeating the spectrum derivation.

nodes.label: Nondegenerate First-Order Perturbation Theory
nodes.explanation: Expand the eigenvalue equation for H₀+λV and derive the first-order energy correction λ⟨n|V|n⟩. Apply it to a small matrix Hamiltonian and compare with the expansion of an exact eigenvalue to see what the approximation controls. Introduce H as the energy operator within the eigenvalue problem. Require an isolated unperturbed level; corrections to eigenvectors, second-order energies, and degenerate subspaces are separate tasks.

nodes.label: Perturbative State Mixing and Second-Order Energies
nodes.explanation: Calculate the first-order admixture of other unperturbed eigenstates and use it to obtain the second-order energy correction. Interpret matrix elements and energy denominators through a two-level example, estimating when mixing becomes too large for the expansion to be useful. Specify normalization to the working order. Connect the energy shift to virtual state mixing without introducing time-dependent transitions or applying the formula at degeneracy.

nodes.label: Degenerate Perturbation Theory
nodes.explanation: Project a perturbation into a degenerate eigenspace, diagonalize that restricted matrix, and identify the appropriate zeroth-order states and first-order splittings. Use a two-dimensional degenerate subspace to show why taking arbitrary diagonal expectations is insufficient. Separate mixing within the degenerate subspace from coupling to other energies. Limit the method to first order and leave near-degenerate resummation and second-order effective Hamiltonians outside the lesson.

nodes.label: The Variational Principle
nodes.explanation: Prove that the normalized energy expectation of an admissible trial state bounds the ground-state energy from above, then optimize a one-parameter trial family. Use a small Hamiltonian first so that trial-state quality and normalization are visible. Explain why the result does not directly bound an arbitrary excited level and why an upper energy bound is not a pointwise wavefunction error bound. Finite-basis generalized eigenvalue methods follow separately.

nodes.label: The Rayleigh–Ritz Method
nodes.explanation: Turn variational optimization over a finite trial subspace into a matrix eigenvalue problem and calculate an approximate ground energy. Include an explicitly computed overlap matrix for a small nonorthogonal basis and explain the generalized equation Hc=ESc. Compare nested subspaces to interpret systematic improvement without assuming prior numerical analysis. Leave rigorous excited-state minimax theorems and large-scale algorithms outside this lesson.

nodes.label: WKB Wavefunctions Away from Turning Points
nodes.explanation: Construct leading semiclassical wavefunctions in allowed and forbidden regions from the local momentum, including the inverse-square-root amplitude. Derive the slowly varying condition and interpret the allowed-region amplitude through probability flux. Use a smooth supplied potential to decide where the approximation is reliable. Do not extend it through a turning point or claim that a single local expression already quantizes the spectrum.

nodes.label: WKB Turning-Point Connection Formulas
nodes.explanation: Match oscillatory and exponential WKB solutions across a simple turning point by locally reducing the equation to the Airy form. Supply the Airy asymptotics and explain which coefficient and phase relations they imply rather than assuming special-function expertise. Practise connecting a decaying tail to the allowed-region solution. Restrict the formulas to smooth isolated linear turning points; hard walls and coalescing turning points require different treatment.

nodes.label: WKB Bound-State Quantization
nodes.explanation: Use two turning-point connections to derive and apply the semiclassical action quantization condition for a smooth confining well. Evaluate the action integral in an accessible example and interpret the half-integer offset as a boundary-phase effect. State the conditions under which the level estimate is reliable. Do not transfer the same offset uncritically to hard-wall or singular potentials.

nodes.label: WKB Tunneling Probabilities
nodes.explanation: Estimate transmission through a smooth forbidden region by integrating the imaginary local momentum between turning points. Connect the result to incoming and outgoing fluxes and compare its exponential dependence with the exact rectangular-barrier result. Distinguish a leading exponential estimate from a controlled prefactor calculation. Restrict the approximation to a sufficiently opaque barrier with well-separated simple turning points.

nodes.label: The Interaction Picture
nodes.explanation: Split H(t)=H₀+V(t), remove the known H₀ evolution, and derive the equation governed by V_I(t). Transform a two-level driving matrix explicitly to see the oscillating energy-gap phases. Introduce a genuinely time-dependent Hamiltonian without assuming that exponentiating an instantaneous matrix solves the general problem. The goal is the change of representation; transition approximations and resonant solutions are developed separately.

nodes.label: First-Order Time-Dependent Perturbation Theory
nodes.explanation: Integrate the interaction-picture equation to obtain first-order transition amplitudes caused by a weak finite-duration perturbation. Calculate a pulse-induced transition and the frequency response of a sinusoidal drive, distinguishing amplitudes from probabilities and diagonal phases. Explain the small-transition-probability limit of the approximation. A transition rate into a continuum and nonperturbative Rabi oscillations are separate outcomes.

nodes.label: Rabi Oscillations and the Rotating-Wave Approximation
nodes.explanation: Reduce a sinusoidally driven two-level Hamiltonian to an approximately constant rotating-frame Hamiltonian and calculate resonant and detuned population oscillations. Define drive amplitude, detuning, and the Rabi-frequency convention explicitly. Explain the rotating-wave approximation and when its neglected fast terms matter. Treat coherent population transfer without relaxation; do not confuse this oscillation with a constant golden-rule transition rate.

nodes.label: Density of States for Free Particles
nodes.explanation: Count large-box one-particle levels in wave-vector space and convert the count into the density of states per unit energy. Derive the dimensional dependence using separable box eigenfunctions and interval or spherical-shell volumes, keeping boundary convention and any supplied internal multiplicity explicit. Explain how a dense discrete spectrum becomes a continuum approximation. This is state counting; thermal particle occupancy is outside this lesson.

nodes.label: Fermi's Golden Rule
nodes.explanation: Obtain a transition rate by combining the long-time peak of a perturbative transition probability with the density of final states. Track units and the energy-conservation condition, including absorption or emission from a prescribed harmonic drive. Explain the time window in which a continuum rate is meaningful even though perturbation theory must remain weak. Do not apply a constant rate to an isolated coherently driven pair of levels.

nodes.label: Electric-Dipole Transition Selection Rules
nodes.explanation: Use the prescribed dipole coupling −q E(t)·r to determine which angular-momentum transitions a chosen field polarization can drive. Combine parity with explicit spherical-harmonic matrix elements to derive the orbital Δl and Δm rules, defining the field and polarization components needed. Distinguish a forbidden matrix element from a small radial overlap. Quantization of the electromagnetic field, spontaneous-emission rates, and general tensor-operator theory are excluded.

nodes.label: The Adiabatic Theorem for Isolated Energy Levels
nodes.explanation: Determine when a state follows an instantaneous nondegenerate energy eigenstate as a Hamiltonian changes, including its accumulated dynamical phase. Expand in the instantaneous basis to relate unwanted transitions to parameter-change rates and spectral gaps, using a slowly swept two-level matrix. State smoothness and gap assumptions explicitly and show why a level crossing defeats a naive slowness claim. Geometric phase is reserved for the next enrichment lesson.

nodes.label: Berry Phase in an Adiabatic Cycle
nodes.explanation: Calculate the geometric phase left after removing the dynamical phase from a closed adiabatic parameter cycle. Use a spin in a slowly rotating magnetic field to evaluate the connection and relate the result to the enclosed solid angle, defining the geometry needed. Explain phase-convention changes and how an interference comparison can reveal the phase. Do not introduce non-Abelian holonomy or topological-band invariants.

nodes.label: Addition of Angular Momentum
nodes.explanation: Construct total angular momentum on a tensor-product space and transform between uncoupled and coupled bases. Determine the allowed total j values and calculate the singlet and triplet states of two spins one-half using highest-weight states and lowering operators. Introduce Clebsch–Gordan coefficients through this concrete computation and state the general coupling range. Extensive coefficient tables and general recoupling symbols are outside the lesson.

nodes.label: Spin–Orbit Coupling
nodes.explanation: Use the supplied effective interaction ξ(r)L·S and the identity relating L·S to J², L², and S² to calculate first-order splittings of hydrogenic levels with l greater than zero. Separate the angular eigenvalue from the radial expectation and identify the coupled basis that diagonalizes the perturbation within the Coulomb degeneracy. Explain the model's physical origin without assuming relativistic field theory, and use a fixed nucleus. The l=0 contact contribution and other fine-structure corrections are separate lessons.

nodes.label: The Leading Relativistic Kinetic-Energy Correction
nodes.explanation: Expand the supplied relativistic free-particle energy at low momentum to identify the −p⁴/(8m³c²) perturbation and calculate its hydrogenic first-order energy shift. Introduce the energy-momentum relation and expansion without assuming special-relativity coursework. Use a fixed nucleus and the unperturbed Schrödinger equation to organize expectations, checking that the perturbation is diagonal in the chosen degenerate manifold. Treat this spin-independent term alone; it is not the full fine-structure result.

nodes.label: The Darwin Contact Interaction
nodes.explanation: Apply the supplied effective Darwin interaction for a fixed point Coulomb source and use the delta sampling rule to evaluate its first-order energy shift. Explain why the contact contribution probes the nucleus and acts only on hydrogenic s states, checking its matrix in the degenerate manifold. State that its coefficient is supplied by low-energy relativistic electron theory rather than deriving that theory here. Exclude finite nuclear size, recoil, and radiative corrections.

nodes.label: Hydrogen Fine-Structure Multiplets
nodes.explanation: Combine the kinetic, spin–orbit, and Darwin corrections into the leading hydrogen fine-structure energy and organize the result by n and total j. Show why all three mechanisms are needed, including the special handling of s states, and interpret the splitting of a low-lying manifold. Use a fixed point nucleus and explicitly neglect recoil at this order of treatment. Distinguish fine structure from the Lamb shift and hyperfine structure rather than attempting either calculation.

nodes.label: The Weak-Field Zeeman Effect
nodes.explanation: Calculate magnetic-field splittings of hydrogenic fine-structure levels using the coupled angular-momentum basis and the Landé factor. Derive the needed magnetic-moment expectation from orbital and spin contributions, keeping sign conventions explicit. State that the field is weak compared with the relevant fine-structure separations. Strong-field recoupling, quadratic Zeeman shifts, and hyperfine effects require different approximations and are excluded.

nodes.label: The Linear Stark Effect in Hydrogen
nodes.explanation: Construct and diagonalize the electric-field perturbation within the degenerate n=2 hydrogen manifold. Use parity and the known orbital wavefunctions to identify and evaluate the relevant z matrix element, then interpret the field-selected combinations and linear energy splitting. Define the electrostatic potential-energy sign convention explicitly. Work in the ideal nonrelativistic Coulomb degeneracy; quadratic shifts and competition with fine structure are outside the lesson.

nodes.label: Density Operators and Statistical Mixtures
nodes.explanation: Represent an ensemble by a positive, unit-trace density operator and compute outcome probabilities and expectations using traces. Compare different ensemble decompositions of the same matrix, calculate purity, and evolve the matrix as UρU†. Teach the trace identity needed for these calculations explicitly. Distinguish an incoherent mixture from a coherent superposition; composite-system reduction and environmental decoherence are separate lessons.

nodes.label: Entanglement and Bell States
nodes.explanation: Determine whether a pure two-system state factors and construct the four Bell states in a product basis. Calculate joint and local measurement probabilities in more than one basis to distinguish entangled correlations from a fixed product preparation or a simple classical mixture. Use only finite-dimensional amplitudes and the established phase rules. Quantitative entanglement measures, reduced density matrices, and Bell inequalities follow separately.

nodes.label: The Partial Trace and Reduced Density Operators
nodes.explanation: Calculate a subsystem's reduced density operator by tracing out a finite environment and verify that it reproduces every local measurement probability. Use an entangled pure state to explain how the subsystem can be mixed while the joint system remains pure. Work through basis-index calculations and show that the choice of basis on the discarded system does not affect the result. Do not interpret reduction as a physical collapse of the joint state.

nodes.label: Schmidt Decomposition of Bipartite Pure States
nodes.explanation: Construct a Schmidt decomposition by diagonalizing a reduced density matrix and finding the corresponding partner states. Use Schmidt rank and the shared nonzero reduced eigenvalues to test and quantify pure-state entanglement, introducing the entropy formula and logarithm convention as a consequence. Practise with a two-qubit state. Mixed-state entanglement measures and multipartite canonical forms are outside the lesson.

nodes.label: The CHSH Bell Inequality
nodes.explanation: Derive the CHSH bound for local hidden-variable assignments and calculate a violating spin correlation for an entangled pair with specified measurement axes. State locality and measurement-setting independence explicitly and connect correlation averages to repeated outcomes. Explain why the violation rules out that combination of assumptions without permitting controllable faster-than-light signaling. Experimental loophole engineering and philosophical interpretation surveys are excluded.

nodes.label: Decoherence from System–Environment Entanglement
nodes.explanation: Evolve a finite system and environment unitarily, trace out the environment, and calculate how environmental-state overlap suppresses off-diagonal elements of the system's reduced matrix. Use a solvable dephasing model to distinguish lost local interference from lost global purity. Explain the dependence on the interaction-selected basis and the possibility of finite-environment recurrences. A master-equation formalism and claims that decoherence alone selects one outcome are outside the lesson.

nodes.label: Generalized Measurements and POVMs
nodes.explanation: Describe a finite measurement through operators M_k, calculate p_k=Tr(M_kρM_k†), and normalize the conditional state. Obtain the effects E_k=M_k†M_k and use an unsharp qubit example to show why the effects specify probabilities but not a unique state update. Motivate the construction with a unitary system-apparatus interaction followed by a projective readout. Continuous measurement records and feedback control are excluded.

nodes.label: Identical Particles and Exchange Symmetry
nodes.explanation: Construct symmetric and antisymmetric two-particle states and explain why relabeling identical particles cannot define a different physical preparation. Introduce the bosonic and fermionic exchange postulates and show how interference of exchanged amplitudes changes joint probabilities. Use orthogonal one-particle states before considering spatial overlap. State the spin-statistics association as physical input; its relativistic proof and thermal occupation distributions are outside nonrelativistic treatment.

nodes.label: Pauli Exclusion and Slater Determinants
nodes.explanation: Build normalized antisymmetric many-fermion states from orthonormal spin-orbitals using Slater determinants and show why repeated occupancy of one spin-orbital makes the state vanish. Introduce the determinant expansion and sign rules directly through two- and three-particle examples. Distinguish a spatial orbital from a spin-orbital when explaining opposite-spin occupancy. Nonorthogonal determinants, creation-operator algebra, and Hartree–Fock self-consistency are excluded.

nodes.label: Singlet–Triplet Spatial Symmetry
nodes.explanation: Combine two-electron spin singlet or triplet states with spatial functions so that the total state has fermionic exchange symmetry. Construct the symmetric and antisymmetric combinations of two spatial orbitals and determine which are compatible with each spin sector. Explain the special case of both electrons in one spatial orbital. Establish the symmetry constraint without yet calculating Coulomb exchange energies or solving a particular atom.

nodes.label: A Variational Ground-State Model of Helium
nodes.explanation: Choose a spin-singlet two-electron trial state built from screened hydrogenic 1s orbitals and minimize its energy over an effective nuclear charge. Set up the kinetic, nuclear-attraction, and electron-repulsion expectations; supply the evaluated repulsion integral so unfamiliar six-dimensional integration does not become a hidden prerequisite. Interpret screening and the remaining correlation error. Use a fixed nucleus and avoid Hartree–Fock or an excited-state exchange calculation.

nodes.label: The Born–Oppenheimer Approximation
nodes.explanation: Separate fast electronic adjustment from slow nuclear motion and construct an effective nuclear potential from a parameter-dependent electronic energy plus nuclear repulsion. Use a supplied one-coordinate electronic energy curve to write and interpret the nuclear equation without assuming molecular chemistry. Work on an isolated electronic surface while neglecting derivative couplings, relate validity to mass scales and gaps, and identify failure near close levels. Detailed nonadiabatic and ab initio calculations are excluded.

nodes.label: Scattering Amplitudes and Cross Sections
nodes.explanation: Identify incoming and outgoing terms in a three-dimensional scattering wavefunction and derive the differential cross section from their probability fluxes. Introduce solid angle, incident flux density, and the total cross section with their physical units, extending the current formula to three dimensions. Use short-range real central potentials and interpret the far-field amplitude. Solving for that amplitude by partial waves or perturbation is left to separate methods.

nodes.label: Partial-Wave Scattering and Phase Shifts
nodes.explanation: Match central-potential radial solutions to free asymptotic waves to determine phase shifts and assemble the scattering amplitude and cross section. Supply the needed free spherical-wave formulas and connect their angular expansion to the known spherical harmonics. Calculate a low-energy s-wave example to make phase shifts observable. Restrict the treatment to elastic scattering by a short-range central potential; Coulomb asymptotics and coupled channels are excluded.

nodes.label: The Lippmann–Schwinger Scattering Equation
nodes.explanation: Rewrite the stationary scattering problem as an integral equation using the outgoing free Green function. Introduce a Green function as the response to a delta source, provide its three-dimensional kernel, and verify the outgoing boundary behavior and source normalization using an explained small-sphere identity. Identify the incident wave and the iterated interaction term. Focus on the integral formulation; the Born truncation and advanced resolvent analysis come later.

nodes.label: The First Born Approximation
nodes.explanation: Replace the exact wave in the Lippmann–Schwinger interaction term by the incident plane wave and obtain the scattering amplitude as a Fourier component of the potential. Define momentum transfer and calculate the angular dependence for a weak finite-range spherical potential. Discuss weak-distortion validity and why strong resonant scattering can defeat the approximation. Keep the scattering expansion distinct from bound-state energy perturbation theory and exclude unscreened Coulomb scattering.

nodes.label: The Optical Theorem for Elastic Scattering
nodes.explanation: Relate the total elastic cross section to the imaginary part of the forward amplitude by using partial-wave unitarity. Work through the phase-shift sum and explain how a forward interference effect accounts for scattering into all angles. Keep normalization and wave-number conventions explicit. Restrict the proof to the already-established short-range elastic setting rather than introducing absorption or a multichannel S matrix.

nodes.label: Scattering of Identical Particles
nodes.explanation: Combine direct and exchanged scattering amplitudes for identical particles in a specified spin-symmetry sector and calculate the resulting distribution for symmetric or antisymmetric spatial states. Explain the interference term and choose a consistent angular-counting convention so equivalent final configurations are not counted twice. Compare with distinguishable-particle scattering using a supplied amplitude. Spin averaging and inelastic multichannel scattering are outside this lesson.

nodes.label: Harmonic-Oscillator Coherent States
nodes.explanation: Construct a normalized annihilation-operator eigenstate in the number basis and evolve its complex amplitude under the oscillator Hamiltonian. Use ladder-operator expectations to calculate the oscillating mean position and momentum and their constant uncertainties. Supply the exponential-series identity needed to normalize the infinite sum. Explain coherent superposition without confusing it with a statistical mixture; quantum-optical field quantization is excluded.

nodes.label: Bloch's Theorem for a Periodic Potential
nodes.explanation: Use discrete translation symmetry to derive the Bloch form of one-dimensional energy eigenfunctions in a periodic potential. Define crystal momentum, its reciprocal-lattice equivalence, and the periodic cell function, then explain what an energy band means using a supplied dispersion. Distinguish crystal momentum from a universally sharp mechanical momentum. Detailed band calculations, electron filling, and topological invariants are outside this lesson.

nodes.label: The Path-Integral Propagator
nodes.explanation: Represent position-space evolution by a propagator kernel and build its composition from short time steps and inserted position resolutions. Introduce the time-sliced nonrelativistic action explicitly, using the free-particle kernel with its oscillatory Gaussian identity supplied. Interpret interference among paths and the stationary-action limit without assuming calculus of variations. This is a working alternative representation, not a rigorous measure construction or a relativistic field path integral.

nodes.label: Resonant Transmission through a Finite Potential Region
nodes.explanation: Calculate above-barrier transmission through a finite rectangular region and identify unit-transmission resonances produced by internal phase accumulation. Interpret the matching result as interference among repeatedly reflected waves and distinguish it from under-barrier suppression. Use a real, lossless one-dimensional potential. Bound-state resonances, decay widths, and multibarrier transfer-matrix machinery are outside this lesson.

nodes.label: Minimal Coupling to Electromagnetic Potentials
nodes.explanation: Construct the Hamiltonian (p−qA)²/(2m)+qφ and distinguish canonical from kinetic momentum for a charged scalar particle. Define the electric and magnetic potentials, introduce the needed gradient and curl components directly, and keep operator ordering explicit when expanding the square. Test the construction in a simple uniform-field gauge. Gauge transformations and magnetic energy quantization are separate lessons; Maxwell theory and spin coupling are not derived here.

nodes.label: Gauge Transformations and Quantum Phase
nodes.explanation: Transform φ, A, and the wavefunction together and verify that the minimally coupled Schrödinger equation and physical probabilities retain their form. Derive the local phase factor with a stated sign convention and extend the probability current to the electromagnetic Hamiltonian, checking gauge-independent kinetic-momentum and flux predictions. Distinguish a position-dependent gauge phase from a constant overall phase. Topological loop effects follow as a separate application.

nodes.label: Landau Levels in a Uniform Magnetic Field
nodes.explanation: Choose a convenient gauge for a uniform magnetic field and reduce the planar orbital Hamiltonian to a shifted harmonic oscillator. Calculate the Landau energies and explain why the oscillator-center parameter labels degeneracy rather than a different energy. Define the cyclotron frequency within this model and distinguish orbital quantization from spin Zeeman splitting. Quantum Hall transport and edge-state calculations are excluded.

nodes.label: The Aharonov–Bohm Phase
nodes.explanation: Calculate the relative phase acquired by two paths enclosing magnetic flux and predict the resulting interference shift when the accessible paths have no magnetic field. Define the line integral through a circular example and explain why the loop phase is gauge invariant even though the vector potential is not. Distinguish a measurable phase difference from a local force on either path. Multiply connected operator domains and a full solenoid scattering solution are excluded.
